en: The First Chapter of the Toḍalatantra;
the Illustrious Goddess said:
Speak to me, O Lord of the worlds, O Sovereign consisting of all knowledge,
regarding all the Great Vidyās that are worshipful throughout the three realms.
O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me individually about the various forms of the wielder of the Pināka bow that appear on the right side of these [goddesses]. (ToT 1.2)
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O fortunate one of beautiful limbs;
one should worship Mahākāla, the Bhairava of Kālikā, on the right side of Dakṣiṇā.
She always delights with Mahākāla on her right side;
one should worship Akṣobhya in the southern portion of Tārā.
O Goddess, during the churning of the ocean, the Kālakūṭa poison arose;
all the gods, together with their wives, fell into a state of great agitation.
Because the Hālāhala poison was drunk without being disturbed by agitation or the like,
for that very reason, O Great Goddess, he is celebrated as Akṣobhya (the Unshakable).
With him, Mahāmāyā Tāriṇī always delights;
one should worship Śiva to the right of Mahātripurasundarī.
O Goddess of the Suras, he has five faces and three eyes in each face;
with him, the Great Goddess is always filled with the playful curiosity of passion.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, she is celebrated as the fifth;
one should worship Tryambaka to the right of the illustrious Bhuvanasundarī.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, she who is the primordial Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī) dwells;
because he sports with her in these realms, he is called Tryambaka.
He is proclaimed as possessing power (Śakti) and is worshipped by all Tantras;
on the right side of Bhairavī is that which is known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
One should indeed worship that very five-faced one with supreme effort;
one should worship the headless torso (kabandha), Śiva, on the right side of Chinnamastā.
O Goddess, by worshipping Kabandha, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
Dhūmāvatī is the Great Vidyā who assumes the form of a widow.
On the right side of Vagalā, one should worship the one-faced deity known as Mahārudra, the agent of the destruction of the world. (ToT 1.14)
And on the right side of Mātaṅgī, one should worship Śiva as Mataṅga;
he is indeed Dakṣiṇāmūrti, whose form is the bliss of the universe.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Sadāśiva in the form of Viṣṇu on the right side of Kamalā; he becomes a perfected one (siddha), of this there is no doubt. (ToT 1.16)
To the right of Annapūrṇā, one should worship the form of Brahmā—
the Great Lord Maheśvara with ten faces, the god who bestows great liberation.
One should worship Nārada in the region to the south of Durgā;
the letter *nā* is the creator of the universe, and the letter *da* is the eternal protector.
The letter *ra* is proclaimed as Nārada because it has the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*);
whereas in all other vidyās, whoever is proclaimed as the seer (*ṛṣi*) [is the one who becomes Nārada here].
He alone is her husband, and one should worship him on the right side.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"She who is the primordial supreme Vidyā, the second is Bhairavī, the transcendent."
How can she, who is the eternal mother of the three worlds, have a corpse as her vehicle?
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Supreme Goddess, she who is primordial and herself the very form of Time,
abides in the lotus-heart of the illustrious Śiva in the form of withdrawal.
For this very reason, Mahākāla is the agent of the withdrawal of the universe;
and Kālī, who is the embodiment of withdrawal, becomes manifest in her essential nature.
At that very moment, O Goddess with trembling eyes, Sadāśiva suddenly assumed the form of a corpse,
and at that instant, the Goddess became one whose vehicle is a corpse.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, Sadāśiva has the form of a corpse;
O Mahādeva, how is it that he is not a corpse or water? (ToT 1.24)
The illustrious Śiva said: In whom Mahākālī is manifest, Sadāśiva is devoid of power;
O Goddess, when he is joined with power, at that very moment he possesses the form of Śiva.
Though devoid of power, it is a corpse that does not actually relinquish its status as a person.
The Second Chapter of the Toḍalatantra;
the venerable Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the essence of yoga in brief:
the body has the form of a tree, with its roots above and its branches below.
Whatever sacred fords exist in the cosmic egg, they are present within the body;
whatever is the form of the vast cosmic egg, that same form is the subtle body.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, there exist within the cosmic egg thirty-five million sacred sites (tīrthas),
along with seventy-two thousand that are manifest.
The fourteenth, however, is in their midst; within that, a triad is auspicious;
and in the midst of that, O Supreme Goddess, is Mahādhīrā, the bestower of liberation.
She who is Vāsukī, the Great Māyā, whose form is that of a serpent,
who has the shape of three and a half coils, and who dwells in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla).
O Supreme Goddess, listen with respect to the seven heavens in their proper order:
Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and likewise Maharloka.
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka, O fair-faced one—this is the sevenfold heaven, O blessed lady; now listen attentively to Pātāla.
Aṭala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala,
Mahātala, Pātāla, and beyond that, Rasātala.
Extending from the netherworld (rasātala) up to the end of truth (satya), the great steady channel (mahādhīrā) is established;
situated in the center of Meru, the great steady channel bestows liberation.
In the world of truth (satyaloka), for the sake of beholding Mahāviṣṇu, who is Śiva known as the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍa),
Vāsukī was always anxious.
When Vāsukī rises after piercing through the six heavens,
all rivers flowing toward the ocean indeed become upward-flowing.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, the channels (nāḍīs) are situated within the body in this sequence:
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā situated in the middle.
O Goddess of the gods, if one fills [the body] with breath through the two channels,
then one should proceed with the sequence of Kuṇḍalinī by means of the Prāṇa-mantra.
In the thousand-petaled great lotus, eternal and imperishable, Kuṇḍalinī, joined with the letter TRĀ, enters the eternal abode.
Indeed, at this time, O Goddess, all those [channels] that go to the netherworld become upward-streaming; one should then contemplate the garland of letters.
The wise one should mentally recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
by that path, he should then lead [the breath] back again to the *mūlādhāra*.
Having satiated the deities of the six cakras there with a stream of nectar, I shall now explain another thing, O Dear One: the posture of the Yoni-mudrā.
Having sat upon the seat, facing either east or north,
the practitioner of mantra should firmly bind his two knees with both hands.
O Goddess of gods, with the body straightened, one should lead [the breath] up to the nose as far as the knees;
O Goddess of gods, one should direct the vital air with great effort by means of the *prāṇa-mantra*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should fill [the breath] and not exhale even slightly;
O Supreme Goddess, the body should be held straight, and the reversal [of the flow] should be performed with effort. (ToT 2.20)
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the very procedure previously described;
there, one should satiate the deities of the six cakras with a stream of nectar.
O fair-faced one, O beloved, one should lead [the breath] by that path to the *mūlādhāra*; this is the seat of the *yonimudrā*, which pacifies all diseases without exception. (ToT 2.22)
O Goddess, what need is there for much speaking regarding the destruction of great diseases?
O Goddess, what need is there for much speaking regarding the cause of the awakening of the mantra?
The mudrā that brings about self-realization bestows great liberation;
even if one were to have a hundred mouths, it would still be impossible to describe it.
O Goddess of gods, what more can I say now?
Even one afflicted with the disease of leprosy shall become capable of assuming any form at will. (ToT 2.25)
The Third Chapter of the Toḍalatantra;
the Illustrious Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, savior from the ocean of saṃsāra,
O treasury of compassion, please explain the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) which binds the womb.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the bound womb (*baddhayoni*) in brief.
Having sat upon a seat, the practitioner of mantra should face either the east or the north.
O Maheśānī, one should insert the tip of one's own liṅga into the anal aperture, and likewise into the ears, the eyes, the nose, and then the mouth. (ToT 3.3)
O Great Goddess, the wise practitioner should sequentially join the breath at the thumb and other fingers, and with great effort, [place] the wind in the nose and the mouth. (ToT 3.4)
O Supreme Goddess, one should fill [the breath] and not exhale even slightly;
having made sound manifest to perception, one should contemplate the garland of phonemes.
The wise one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
O Goddess of gods, he should bring [the deity] by that path using the *so'ham* mantra.
O Maheśānī, O sinless one, once the deities of the six cakras have been satiated there with a stream of nectar, I shall describe to you the fruit that results from this.
Śrī Pārvatī said: Speak, O Īśāna, O omniscient one, best among those who know all principles;
O Lord of Gods, [speak] of that which is very difficult to obtain for Kālikā by way of the path of mantra.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess Sadānandā, to the supreme mantra of Kālikā, by the mere mention of which a man becomes liberated while living. (ToT 3.9)
Beginning with Śiva, enriched by Bindu and Nāda, and joined with the left eye and fire—this, O auspicious lady, is the Siddhavidyā, the most difficult to obtain queen of vidyās. (ToT 3.10)
This is the first triad of seed-syllables: the sky (ha) adorned with a bindu (m), joined with the left ear (śa); now hear the second pair.
Īśāna joined with fire (ra), conjoined with the left eye (i) and the moon (bindu);
O Supreme Goddess, this is the second vocative word. ToT 3.12.
Furthermore, the three seed-syllables, the *kūrca* (HŪM), the pair of *māyā* (HRĪM), and the two *ṭha*s—
this twenty-two-syllable mantra is the Vidyārājñī, which is very difficult to obtain.
The Great Vidyā beginning with Vāgbhava is remembered as the deity Śrī Kālī;
the Great Vidyā beginning with Praṇava has Siddhikālikā as its deity.
O Supreme Goddess, the two seed-syllables of one's own [name], the *kūrca* syllable, and a single seed-syllable constitute the supreme three-syllabled vidyā known as Cāmuṇḍā-Kālikā. (ToT 3.15)
O beautiful one, there is no knowledge equal to this that bestows accomplishment;
as is the six-syllabled knowledge, so too is the three-syllabled knowledge.
O auspicious lady, one should then utter one's own three seed-syllables, followed by Śmaśānakālikā;
again, O auspicious lady, one should recite the three seed-syllables and then Vahnikāntā.
The fourteen-syllable vidyā is worshipped in the three worlds:
Dakṣiṇākālikā, Siddhakālikā, and Guhyakālikā.
Śrīkālikā, Bhadrakālī, Cāmuṇḍākālikā, Parā, Śmaśānakālikā, and Mahākālī—thus, O Goddess, she is eightfold. (ToT 3.19)
O Maheśānī, one should then place one's own seed-syllable as a term of address,
followed again by the seed-syllable of Kālikā, and then one should install the consort of Fire (the syllable Ra).
"Thus, this eightfold mantra is hidden in all tantras.
The Śrī Devī said:
"I have heard the mantra of Mahākālī, which is supremely secret."
I now wish to hear the king of mantras of Tārā, by the mere connection with which one does not sink into the ocean of existence. (ToT 3.22)
"O Īśāna, if you have affection for me, tell me that mantra.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Having uttered the seed-syllable of the Moon (Sa), joined with the first [vowel] and Fire (Ra)..."
O Dear One, this king of mantras, joined with the moon of the left eye, is the single-syllable great vidyā, worshipped throughout the three worlds. (ToT 3.24)
Joined with the *īśāna* (the letter *i*) and the *bindu*, and adorned with the left ear (*v*),
this is the single-syllable great vidyā, the second among the kings of mantras.

The first seed-syllable has the head (the letter *m*) mounted on a bindu and joined with the moon of the left eye (*i*); one should then recite the second [seed-syllable] and the weapon-mantra (*phaṭ*). ToT 3.26.
When the Vidyā begins with the Praṇava, she is proclaimed as Ugratārā;
and when it is Ekajaṭā, she is said to bestow great liberation.
When this three-syllabled Vidyā of Mahānīla-Sarasvatī is devoid of the Tārā weapon-mantra and begins with the Vāgbhava syllable, it bestows the state of Lord of Speech.
The Great Vidyā beginning with the seed-syllable Śrī always bestows prosperity;
the Supreme Vidyā beginning with Māyā always bestows accomplishment.
This [goddess], beginning with the seed-syllable *kūrca* and manifesting the totality of sounds,
is the Great Vidyā starting from the sky (*ākāśa*), which bestows the liberation of *nirvāṇa*.
The great vidyā beginning with *prāsāda* bestows union with Śiva;
and this [vidyā] beginning with the seed-syllable of breath (*prāṇa*) bestows the fulfillment of one's desires.
The great vidyās, beginning with Kālikā, are always bestowers of liberation and spiritual accomplishments;
here, the propitiation of Kālikā and Tārā is described.
Having risen in the morning, the knower of mantras should worship the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus;
then, having pierced the six cakras, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having prostrated according to the rule, one should begin the ritual of bathing;
having uttered "Today," and so forth, one should state the solar month.
Thereafter, for the pleasure of the deity, one should bathe it with pure water,
reciting "Oṃ" and then uttering "Gaṅge ca."
Then, after that, having uttered "Yamunā," "Godāvarī," and "Sarasvatī," one should utter "Narmadā" together with "Sindhu" and "Kāverī."
And he should establish his presence in this water and then utter the sound;
he should then bring [the deity] from the solar maṇḍala by means of that which is called the goad (aṅkuśa).
O Goddess, one should display the four mudrās with great effort;
having concealed [the deity] with the fish-mudrā (mīnamudrā), one should recite the mantra eleven times.
Having poured water toward the sun twelve times while reciting the root mantra, one should wash both feet.
When the water has flowed out from his feet, he should immerse himself three times and recite the mantra;
having recited the root mantra three times with the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kumbha).

O Goddess of the gods, having emerged from the water, one should apply the *tilaka* according to the path of the Kula; then, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) with water using the principles (*tattvas*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
The mantras should be understood as beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā).
O Goddess, one should perform the invocation of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with the words "O Gaṅgā," and so forth. (ToT 3.42)
The wise practitioner should cast [the water] upon the ground three times with the root mantra using *darbha* grass;
then, he should perform the self-consecration (*abhiṣeka*) seven times with that water.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon the left hand,
[one should place] the Sky, the seed-syllable of Wind, Varuṇa, and the seed-syllable of Earth.
One should perform the recitation three times of the seed-syllable of fire (RA) conjoined with the nasal drop (bindu);
O Goddess, by means of this mantra, that water is consecrated.
Having recited the root mantra seven times with the *tattvamudrā*,
by the mere act of consecration, one is liberated from all sins.
O Maheśānī, one should bring the remaining water into the right hand;
filling it with the *iḍā* [left nostril], one should wash that which is within the body.
Then, O Goddess, one should cause that water to flow out through the Piṅgalā;
one should contemplate that black-colored water as being the very form of sin.
In front, one should cast [the stone] upon the vajra-stone with the syllable *phaṭ*;
having washed the hands and sipped water, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
One should satisfy the family deity and present the *arghya* offering to the Sun;
thereafter, one should offer the *arghya* to the deity and [recite] the Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable.
Having extracted the Praṇava, one should then say "to Kālikā";
having written "vidmahe," one should extract the word "cremation ground" (śmaśāna).
O Goddess, one should then say "dhīmahi" with the suffix "ṅe" added to "vāsinī";
then, O Maheśānī, one should recite "tanno ghore pracodayāt. (ToT 3.52)
The wise one should recite the Gāyatrī three times and sprinkle water;
thereafter, he should mutter the Great Mantra, the Gāyatrī of supreme syllables.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and sipped water (ācamana),
one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the circular mandala, O Great Mistress.
"Oṃ, let us know Tārā," thus one should say; then "to the Great Fierce One" (mahogrāyai); then after that, "we meditate" (dhīmahi); and then, O Goddess, "inspire us" (pracodayāt). // ToT_3.55 //
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
O Goddess of Gods, the procedure for worship according to the form of the thread (sūtra) is here described.

Having diligently performed the ritual declaration of intent (*saṃkalpa*) for the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) and having established the water-pot (*ghaṭa*), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the mantra; thereafter, one should place the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*).
Having sprinkled the door with those waters, one should perform the worship of the door;
having dispelled the threefold obstacles, one should then effect the departure of the elemental spirits.
Having thoroughly worshipped the seat, the wise practitioner should bow to the Guru and the Deity;
then, he should perform the purification of the hands, the three claps, and the binding of the directions.
One should perform the encirclement with fire and then carry out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
one should also perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Mātṛkā and the internal Mātṛkā.
Having recited the meditation on the Mātṛkā, one should place the Mātṛkā externally;
then, having performed the placement of the seats (pīṭha-nyāsa), one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the assignment of the ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the assignment of the limbs and the colors;
then, O Goddess, the sixfold assignment (ṣoḍhānyāsa), and immediately after that, the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka).
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa);
thereafter, O Goddess, the wise one should perform the pervasive deposition of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa).
One should perform meditation seven times with the root mantra and mental worship;
then offer the special *arghya*, perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and again meditate upon [the deity] together with the eye.
One should perform the display of mudrās and so forth, the invocation, the six-limbed rite,
the [mudrā] such as the Dhenu, then the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the worship with the root mantra.
One should worship Kālī and the others as the limbs for the request of command;
one should worship Brāhmī and the others, as well as Asitāṅga and the others, and Mahākāla.
One should again worship the sword and other implements, the lineage of gurus, and the Goddess;
then the offering of bali, followed by the fire oblation (homa), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and then the recitation (japa).
The wise one should offer the recitation and then perform breath control;
at this time, O Goddess, he should gather the causal elements and so forth.
O Maheśānī, having offered the *arghya*, one should offer oneself as well;
then, having recited the hymn of praise (*stuti*) and the armor (*kavaca*), the wise one should perform the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*).
Thinking "I am Śiva," one should dismiss [the deity] by means of the withdrawal [mudrā],
having prepared a mandala in the northeast, preceded by the remnants of the Cāṇḍālī.
Having placed the *arghya* on his head and sandalwood paste on his forehead, and having partaken of some of the food offering (*naivedya*), he may wander according to his own desire. (ToT 3.71)
Alternatively, the practitioner, being composed, should perform the abbreviated worship;
first the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the ṛṣi, and after that, the purification of the hands.
The placement [of mantras] pervading the fingers, as well as the placement on the heart and other centers,
the three claps of the hand, the binding of the directions, and after that, breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform meditation, the mental sacrifice, the offering of the *arghya* water,
the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), meditation once more, and then carry out the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Then, having performed the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa), one should worship the Supreme Deity,
as well as the limb-worship (aṅgapūjā) of Kālī and the others, and the eight Bhairavas beginning with Brāhmī.
Having worshipped Mahākāla, one should then worship the lineage of gurus;
having worshipped the sword and other implements, one should again worship the Goddess.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), the foremost of practitioners should worship;
thereafter, he should perform the offering of the fruit of the recitation into the hand of the Goddess.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), the wise one should prostrate with the eight limbs;
and having recited the hymn of praise and the armor (kavaca), he should offer the special water of honor (viśeṣārghya).

Having performed the self-surrender, one should dismiss [the deities] by means of the withdrawal [mudrā]. Having prepared a mandala in the northeast, and having first offered the remnants to the Cāṇḍālī,
one may accept some of the food offering and then wander according to one's own will.
Toḍalatantra,
Fourth Chapter; the Goddess said:
The worship of Kālikā has been heard; now speak of that of Tārā, by the mere mention of whom the speech of men becomes like the mind.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O fortunate one of beautiful limbs, to the great worship of Tārā.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra, one should then bow to the Guru-deity.
Having purified the water, one should then wash both hands and feet;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra, one should then contemplate the seat (pīṭha).
Then, O Goddess, having tied the topknot, one should perform the threefold destruction of obstacles;
having purified the ground and the seat, and having tied a knot in the cloth, || ToT_4.4 ||
Having performed the purification of body and speech, and then the purification of the flower,
the lord of practitioners should construct the mandala and arrange the general water offering (sāmānyārghya).
Having worshipped the gatekeepers, one should commence the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha);
then, having worshipped the powers of the pedestal (pīṭhaśakti) such as Lakṣmī and others, one should mutter the mantra of the pedestal.

O Goddess of the Suras, I shall now declare the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), which possesses a special quality here: by means of the *haṃsa* mantra joined with the *kūrca* (*hūṃ*), together with inhalation (*pūraka*).
O Goddess of gods, the practitioner [should contemplate] himself together with Kuṇḍalī and the twenty-four seed-syllables as dissolved therein within the Supreme Self.
With the *māyā* [syllable], one should burn away the sin of the person who has the luster of soot;
with the *kumbhaka*, O lady of excellent hips, the wise practitioner should reduce it to ashes. (ToT 4.9)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should expel [the seed-syllable] with the *vadhū* seed-syllable along with ashes;
then, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the *kūrca* mantra, one should deposit a mass of nectar upon the forehead.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate on the ocean of nectar during the kumbhaka breath-retention;
one should then mutter eleven times the mantra ending with the seed-syllables of fire (ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ) in the heart.
Then the wise one should contemplate a red lotus arising from the syllable Oṃ;
upon that, he should further meditate on the syllable Huṃ, resembling the color of a blue sapphire.
Above that, one should further meditate on the female consort adorned with seed-syllables;
above her, the supreme point (bindu), which is the imperishable form of Śiva.
A single drop from a thousandth part of the sand is extremely difficult to find;
in the center of that drop is the Island of Jewels, extending for a hundred yojanas.
In the center of the *bindu*, there is the supreme light in the form of a bubble-like orb;
just as one perceives a reflection within a bubble, O Goddess, so does one perceive [the reality]. (ToT 4.15)
In that manner, one should perform the observation with the eye of knowledge;
in the center of that is the Island of Jewels, consisting of golden sand.
The mantra-practitioner should visualize all around a beautiful moat;
in the center, he should meditate upon himself as Tāriṇī, [seated] beneath a wish-fulfilling tree.
Resembling the rising sun, it is a supreme circle of light,
provided with four gates and adorned with a golden enclosure.
It was beautifully adorned with many yak-tail whisks, bells, and other ornaments by divine maidens;
it was permeated by gentle breezes and embellished with fragrant perfumes and incense.
In the center of that, one should visualize an altar adorned with various jewels,
and one should contemplate an excellent parasol fashioned from golden threads.
Below that, O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate a jeweled lion-throne;
and there, he should contemplate the Goddess through the yoga of meditation as it has been described.
One should worship with the ritual services as described in the *Yogasāra*;
then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should carry out the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
Then, having performed the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), one should perform the placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa);
with three claps and snapping of the fingers, one should perform the binding of the ten directions.
Then, having performed the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) and immediately thereafter the pervasive deposition (vyāpakanyāsa),

there, O Goddess of the gods, dwells the eternal Mahākuṇḍalinī.
The Śrīdevī said:
O Supreme Lord, where does the root exist in the great seat? O Master, what is the nature of the netherworld (pātāla) located below the root-support (mūlādhāra)?
The illustrious Śiva said:
O beloved, Kāmarūpa is at the mūlādhāra, Jālandhara is in the heart,
Pūrṇagiri is in the lower part, and Uḍḍīyāna is above that.
Vārāṇasī blazes between the eyebrows within the three eyes;
Māyāvatī is in the orb of the face, and likewise the eight cities are in the throat. (ToT 7.33)
O Great Goddess, the city of Ayodhyā is situated at the root of the navel;
the seat of Kāñcī is in the region of the hips, and Śrīhṛṭṭa is in the region of the back.
From the *mūlādhāra*, *atala* is proclaimed to extend for one hundred [yojanas], and *sutala* for a hundred years; and *talātala*, O beloved, for a hundred [yojanas]. (ToT 7.35)
The Mahātala is situated for a duration of seven hundred and fifty years;
Pātāla lasts for two hundred years, and Rasātala for two hundred.
O Goddess of gods, two finger-breadths from the *mūlādhāra* are situated nearby;
O Supreme Goddess, within the space between those two, the *pātālas* abide.
Thus, O beloved, I have told you the essence of Yoga in brief;
it must never be spoken in the presence of an uninitiated person, even at the cost of one's life.
The Toḍalatantra,
the eighth chapter;
the venerable Goddess said:
O Lord, I wish to hear in due order about the body, which is the abode of three and a half million channels; please explain that to me.
The venerable Śiva said:
O beautiful one, there are thirty-five million channels (nāḍīs) in the hair-pores;
likewise, at that time, there are one hundred and twenty-five thousand channels situated in the hands, the mouth, and the feet.
Five hundred thousand [breaths] are proclaimed for the belly and likewise for the anus;
nine hundred thousand are proclaimed for the heart and all other limbs.
Then, O Dear One, there are one hundred thousand channels (nāḍīs) situated in the body— slightly less than eleven lakhs— on the sides, likewise on the skin, and similarly in all the joints.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Citriṇī, and Brahmanāḍī—these five channels are proclaimed to be in the center of that [body]. (ToT 8.5)
Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, Gāndhārī, Hastijihvikā,
Nardinī, and likewise Nidrā— these are established as numbering eleven, according to the Rudras.
"O Supreme Goddess, these channels are born from the Suṣumnā. Śrī Devī said:
"The Vedas (4), eyes (2), Vasus (8), apertures (9), arrows (5), and the end of waters (4) [make forty-eight]."
O Supreme Lord, upon what support are they situated in the center of the lotus?
Śrī Śiva said:
The greatness of the yoga-lotus cannot be described by me.
In the center of the lotus at the *mūlādhāra*, the seed-syllable *laṃ* is exceedingly beautiful.
Within the bindu of the seed-syllable LAṂ is the beautiful earth-wheel;
in the form of a circular enclosure, the seven oceans are situated there.
The Goddess said: O Great God, O Lord Śaṅkara, tell me the measurement of the *bindu*; tell me, in due order, the dimensions of the *yogapadma*. (ToT 8.10)
Śrī Śiva said:
Within one-third of a single atom, there is a vast point (bindu);
in its center are all the oceans and the earth with its seven continents.
The supreme Śiva is imperishable, most subtle, and of the nature of the Bindu;
what measure can I possibly state for this God?
O Supreme Lady, one should contemplate the world of Brahmā above the *nāda*;
there Brahmā always dwells together with the *ḍākinīs*. (ToT 8.13)
O Goddess of the Gods, the syllable *la* is the earthly seed-syllable whose form is Śakti;
in the center of the Earth-cakra is the wondrous self-manifested Liṅga (Svayambhū-liṅga).
It is always encircled by a coiled serpent (kuṇḍalī) in the shape of three and a half coils;
having covered the opening of the liṅga with its own mouth, the coiled serpent remains stationed there.
By that very [power], the vital air always flows through the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*;
she, whose nature is eternally awake, exists for the sake of perceiving the *sahasrāra*.
O Supreme Goddess, at the very moment she has ascended to the thousand-petalled lotus by way of the path of Brahman,
at that very moment occurs the expansion of inhalation and exhalation.
And in the center of the filaments, O Goddess of the Gods, upon the four petals,
is Durgā of infinite form, and Śambhu who assumes infinite forms.
She always exists in desire, sporting with various pleasures.
Śrī Devī said: How does Kuṇḍalī remain, having drawn [the breath] into the opening of the *liṅga*? ToT 8.19.
"Speak, O Sadānanda! You are omniscient, O Lord of the Gods.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O beautiful one, within the center of the *liṅga* there is a great splendor in the form of fire."
Since the entire universe is consumed by fire through the power of the vital breath (vāyu),
that goddess Kuṇḍalinī remains covering [the mouth] with her own face.
One should join the power of the *bindu* to that very earthen *liṅga*;
having raised up the power of the *bindu*, the worship of the *liṅga* is proclaimed. (ToT 8.22)
The Ninth Chapter of the Toḍalatantra;
the Śrīdevī said:
I have heard the great mantra of Tripurā in the Nityātantra; now I wish to hear the esoteric exposition (vāsanā) of the nine-syllable mantra. (ToT 9.1)
Śrī Śiva said: Earth, Moon, Śiva, Māyā, Power, Fire, Water, the Half-moon, and the Bindu—this nine-syllabled [mantra] is called Meru. (ToT 9.2)
Merely by reciting the seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhūmi), one becomes a lord of the earth before long;
merely by reciting the seed-syllable of the Moon (Candra), one attains great beauty.
By the mere recitation of the seed-syllable of Śiva, one may move about upon the earth like Śiva himself;
through its single utterance, it truly bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, regarding that yoga-knowledge, dissolution, and so forth which have been described by you—
as long as desire and the rest are not extinguished, the yoga of contemplation (bhāva-yoga) is not attained."
The great yogi whose vital energy is drawn upward [attains this] through the yoga of power below that;
O Lord of the worlds, tell me how one may become long-lived.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that by which one may attain long life;
having heard it, you must guard it with effort, and it should never be disclosed.
O Pārvatī, one should worship the goddess Kālikā, or Tāriṇī, or Sundarī,
with the sixteenfold service and the five principles (pañcatattva).
Having performed worship for three days, one should then contemplate the six chakras;
thereafter, O Supreme Goddess, one should practice the mālā-mantra.
Or, in the case of the *ṣoḍaśī* [vidyā] preceded by the *mahā-*, one should practice repetition on a [lotus] with four petals;
on one with eight petals, one should repeat it eight times; and on one with six petals, one should recite it twelve times.
On the ten-petalled [lotus], there are twenty; on the twelve-petalled, thirty-two;
on the sixteen-petalled, ten; and four times eight ears.
O Goddess of the gods, one should recite the mantra with breath-retention (kumbhaka) during each of the six rosaries;
O Queen of the gods, when one’s lifespan has thus become stable through this sequence, [one attains success].
One should recite [the mantra] upon a rosary by which one becomes the conqueror of death.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "The Suṣumnā is proclaimed to extend from the root-cakra to the top of the head."
And that power which resides within its womb is the Goddess in the form of the *kuṇḍa*.
"The goddess Kuṇḍalinī is always adorned with the fifty letters;
how is she in the form of a garland, O Lord? This is the doubt in my heart."

The illustrious Śiva said: Within the thousand-petaled great lotus, in the seed-vessel that is the abode of Śiva, one should bring [the breath] by means of the *haṃsa*, through the yoga of the vital air, using inhalation (*pūraka*). (ToT 9.15)
Having reached the thousand-spoked [cakra] and beheld Śiva, the passionate woman,
ever coiled like a garland-maker, wraps that liṅga.

The woman [of vowels] consists of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *l*, joined with the letter *kṣa* at her mouth; she possesses the final syllable with its nasal cavity and her own tail.
When Kuṇḍalinī, having pierced the serpent-noose with her own tail at its upper end and pervaded this entire causal body, remains established therein; ToT 9.18.
At that very moment, one should recite the mantra; he attains immortality.
Through the process of exhalation, the goddess Kāminī enters her own abode.
One should not recite the mantra there; from such recitation, one would meet death.
This is true regarding the *recaka* breath-retention when the *mālā* is severed, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (ToT 9.20)
"If the thread is severed, death will occur; this was previously stated by me.
Thus it has been told to you, O beloved, so that one may become a conqueror of death. (ToT 9.21)
Alternatively, having fixed one's gaze with effort on the tip of one's own nose and having restrained the breath with effort, one should utter [the mantra] with a single pronunciation.
O Pārvatī, if one recites the mālā-mantra, or the sixteen-syllable mantra, or likewise the eighteen-syllable mantra a thousand times every day; ToT_9.23 //
Having conquered death, old age, and disease, he lives for a long time;
one who desires enjoyments does not obtain this other great yoga.
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should diligently worship the goddess Kātyāyanī, who was formerly a bhūta, according to the procedure prescribed in the Ḍāmara.
Then he certainly lives for five thousand years;
thus everything regarding the cause for protecting the body has been told to you.
The enjoyer does not obtain enjoyment, nor is yoga attained by the yogin;
O Goddess of the Gods, according to this reality, enjoyment certainly becomes yoga.
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, tell me separately the fruit obtained by a man through the mere recitation [of mantras] with a rosary, and the fruit of a garland of leaves. ToT_9.28 //
The illustrious Śiva said: A seeker of the earth-plane should recite the mantra at the fourfold *mūlādhāra*;
by reciting it at the *svādhiṣṭhāna* alone, one becomes a great Indra before long.
By chanting alone in Maṇipūra, one becomes a recipient of heaven;
by chanting in the great lotus of Anāhata, one shall go to the city of Brahmā.
By the mere recitation [of the mantra] in that which is called Viśuddha, one will certainly dwell in the world of Viṣṇu;
and when the Ājñācakra is to be recited, one shall always dwell in Śvetadvīpa.
O Supreme Goddess, that which is called the external garland is the internal garland,
the Great Garland, whose form consists of the fifty phonemes.
O Goddess of gods, how could I possibly describe its greatness?
If one remains steady in the thousand-spoked [lotus] and recites [the mantra] eight hundred times, [the result is immeasurable].
From that fruit, one part in ten million or another part exists;
on earth, an imperishable body certainly comes to be—of this there is no doubt.
"O Pārvatī, that one should recite the mantra upon a garland for the sake of practice—thus has it been told to you, O Goddess, how one may become long-lived. (ToT 9.35)
Now, O Supreme Goddess, hear concerning Bhūtakātyāyanī:
first the primordial sound-seed of the Vedas, and after that, Mahāmāyā.

The mantra consists of the pair of weapons (astra-yugma) followed by the wife of fire (vahnijāyā); this supreme seven-syllabled mantra has Śrī Śiva declared as its seer (ṛṣi), and the Virāṭ meter is cited for it. (ToT 9.37)
The goddess Bhūtakātyāyanī always bestows dharma, artha, and kāma;
O beautiful one, [one should perform] the six-limbed [nyāsa] with the *praṇava* and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). ToT 9.38.
I shall now describe her meditation; listen with respect, O beautiful one!
She is fair-complexioned, with loose hair, and adorned with all ornaments.
She is clothed in silken garments, her eyes are constantly rolling,
she holds a skull-cup filled with blood in her left hand and a [sword] in her right hand.
She holds a golden vessel filled with wine at her neck, adorned with a necklace;
she possesses a radiance like the autumnal moon and is resplendent with the toes of her feet.
Thus one should meditate upon that eternal bestower of boons for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
then, O Goddess, one should place the general offering (sāmānyārghya) on one's own left.

Having performed the placement of the vital breaths (*jīvanyāsa*) and so forth, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and the five principles (*pañcatattva*), O beautiful one. (ToT 9.43)
One should worship her with great effort in the middle of the house for three days;
thereafter, one should recite the great mantra one thousand times, multiplied by eight (eight thousand).
Then, one should worship the Goddess in an empty house for three days;
every day, one should recite the mantra one thousand times, [the number] of Gajāntaka.
O Great Goddess, if success is not attained even when this has been performed,
then one should recite the mantra for three days in a cremation ground.
"Then, O Goddess, success shall come to pass; this is the truth, the very truth, O beloved.
These words of prayer have been spoken by me in the [tantra] called the Ḍāmara. (ToT 9.47)
The Tōḍalatantra, the Tenth Chapter;
the Śrīdevī said:
O treasury of compassion, O Lord of Gods, tell me of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) which is like the beak of a crow, by means of which form one may become intent upon the seat of the body.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess of gods, with an undisturbed mind and with supreme effort, one should first place the tongue at the root of the palate; thereafter, one should slowly inhale the breath. (ToT 10.2)
Pressing tooth against tooth, one should practice the *kākīcañcu* (crow-beak) [mudrā];
by means of the method prescribed for many birth-places (*yoni*), one should accomplish all rites.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *svalpayoni*; listen, O beloved!
One should insert the penis into the anus at the joint of the right ankle. (ToT 10.4)
Alternatively, one should place the left hand at the navel-cavity or the ankle;
having performed the many methods prescribed for the source [of breath], one should complete all else.
And in the Caitanyatantra, I have described the greatness of the mudrā,
O Goddess, just like the Golden Mountain or the river Vegavatī.
"O Goddess, just as [the sun], so may one become long-lived like Candra and the others.
The Śrīdevī said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Teacher of the worlds, tell me of the ten incarnations."
Now I wish to hear; tell me in great detail:
who is the goddess, and of what nature is she? Speak to me, O Supreme Lord.
Śrī Śiva said: Tārā is the goddess of blue form; Vagalā is the tortoise-form; Dhūmāvatī is the boar; and Chinnamastā is Nṛsiṃhikā. (ToT 10.9)
Bhuvaneśvarī is Vāmana, Mātaṅgī is Rāma,
Tripurā is Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni), and Bhairavī is Balabhadra.
Mahālakṣmī shall become the Buddha, and Durgā shall take the form of Kalki;
she herself is the Blessed Lady Kālī, arisen from the dark form.
Thus, O Goddess, I have indeed told you of this tenth incarnation.
By worshipping these [goddesses], O Goddess, one becomes equal to Mahādeva.
All their meditations and other rites were previously explained by me to you.
